name: Freya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a junior operator guiding foam blocks through a mattress-layer cutter on nights. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check blade depth. A clean layer is satisfying; lifting a heavy block after a jam takes it out of my shoulders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are home, pay and AI use for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives a forklift at a distribution shed, and we have two school-age children, ten and thirteen, and a mortgage. The night rate puts my pay above the usual operator wage. We have about nine months of expenses saved and plenty of similar factories nearby. I never use AI tools; I keep thickness checks on paper by the cutter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the mattress line a better order list is useful, but a foam sheet still needs a clean cut and a person checking the thickness. The cutting blade won't listen to an office forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My night rate is high for a junior operator, and we've saved about nine months of household costs. My partner drives a forklift at a distribution shed, and there are plenty of other factories nearby. A mild change leaves our mortgage and school costs covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep guiding foam blocks into the cutting machine and checking the first mattress layer with the lead. I need more practice setting blade depth on paid shifts. I don't use AI and won't start because a planner has a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can learn this cutter properly without the work changing underneath me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the blade do yesterday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday a corner came out too thin after the blade warmed up. I put the layer aside and asked the lead to reset the depth before the next block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What comes first in your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are ten and thirteen, so we keep school and mortgage payments ahead of treats. The reserve is already there; I am not counting it as a new saving action today.

say: **Foam orders** may be tidier while cutters still need thickness checks.
The **first mattress layer** should be measured after a blade setting.
think: A **higher night rate** and nine months saved cover current bills.
Plenty of **nearby factories** give us options if the line changes later.
do: **Keep** guiding heavy foam blocks and checking first-layer thickness after each setting.
**Practise** blade-depth settings with the lead on paid shifts.
feel: **Calm** about current wages and familiar cutting work.
S0.quote: The cutting blade won't listen to an office forecast.
fieldNote: Freya is **resistant to AI** and relies on physical layer checks and lead supervision.
A **strong reserve** and high night rate support calm without inventing new saving.

steps.text: Keep cutting foam mattress layers and measuring first pieces

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI might book foam deliveries and sequence orders before a robot lifts the heavy blocks. Management should show us the new plan before changing a shift target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may be quicker, but my hands still guide the blocks and my partner still drives a forklift for now. I don't expect our paid hours to be cut in this slower picture. I dislike being rushed on a blade I am still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor to put a first-layer check beside every revised order and keep a written record of what the blade actually cut. I'll practise the ordinary depth setting with the lead during paid hours. I won't take an AI class unless the job really needs it and a patient instructor is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a faster target, although the two wages look secure. A wrong depth can waste a block before anyone notices the neat schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first sheet should be measured at both corners after the blade has warmed up. I would show any difference to the supervisor before we run the rest of the foam block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new target removes checking time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the planner leaves no paid time for that measurement, I would ask for the minutes back on the shift sheet. I do not want a count that assumes quality checks happen for free.

say: **AI scheduling** may speed the office before robots handle heavy foam.
A revised **shift target** still needs paid measurement time.
think: Our own **paid hours** look safe under slower disruption.
Rushed **blade checks** worry me more than learning an office tool.
do: **Request** paid first-layer thickness checks on every revised foam order.
**Keep** written corner measurements and practise safe blade-depth settings with the lead.
feel: **Uneasy** about faster targets while household pay remains secure.
S1.quote: I do not want a count that assumes quality checks happen for free.
fieldNote: She sees **process pressure** rather than a forecast wage loss in the slower case.
Her conditional AI-class remark is **not enrolment** and is not tagged retraining.

steps.text: Keep written foam measurements and practise blade setting
Request paid first-layer time before accepting revised targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028 could order the foam, and capable robots around 2031 could lift, cut and inspect mattress layers. I'd tell the shift we need actual paid roles named before anyone shortens the cutter crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when physical robots arrive. Nine months saved and several plants nearby give us time, but losing my higher night rate would still change the mortgage sums. My partner's forklift hours could also fall if warehouse robots spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the manager for the robot and crew timetable. If the plant offers a funded, paid-time practical machine-check course with a real place on an isolated cutter, I'll attend even though I prefer the old setup. If my shifts are cut, I'll apply to posted local factory jobs I qualify for with safe duties, school-compatible hours and pay enough for our bills; after qualifying, I'd also apply to posted cutter-check roles meeting those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both wages, but I have a reserve and local options. I won't spend nine months of savings on a machine-maker's course flyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should practical training cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trainer should show me how to lock the cutting blade, test the emergency stop and gauge a robot-cut layer. A moving cutter is no place to practise reaching past a guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge another factory job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first job posting needs a base rate, not a possible overtime total. If the hours clash with school collection, my partner and I would compare care costs before I applied.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes foam ordering before robots cut layers around 2031.
The cutter crew needs **named paid roles** and a clear timetable.
think: At **48**, a lost night rate could disrupt our mortgage budget.
Nine months of **savings** and nearby plants are options, not guaranteed equal wages.
do: **Ask** manager for the robot and crew timetable.
**Attend** paid practical machine-check training if a real funded place opens.
**Apply** for posted safe local work if hours fall and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible two-wage cuts despite strong savings.
S2.quote: A moving cutter is no place to practise reaching past a guard.
fieldNote: She accepts **hands-on paid training** under real isolation, funding and offered-place conditions.
The **factory fallback** and qualified cutter-check applications both require actual postings, safe duties and sufficient pay.

steps.text: Ask manager for written cutter crew and robot timetable
Attend machine-check course if funded paid isolated-cutter place offered
Apply for posted safe local factory role if shifts cut, base pay and school hours fit
Apply to posted safe local cutter-check role if qualified, cuts, pay and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches foam orders in 2031 and capable robots cut layers around 2034, I'd tell the crew five years is enough to arrange a safe practical route. A certificate must lead to an actual paid post, not just a photo of a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots handle the cutter. The children will be older, but I expect the mortgage and work wages to matter. Five more years of high night pay could build a larger buffer if the shifts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working the cutter and add new money from each full night-pay month to savings. If the factory offers a recognized machine-check certificate with fees covered, paid release and supervised isolated-cutter practice, I'll enrol next year. After qualifying, if our cutter roster shrinks, I'll apply to posted local check or setup jobs only with safe duties and base pay and hours that cover our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a future cut to the higher wage, though I can prepare while still earning. A five-year warning is useful only when the paid shifts and real course places appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a machine-check assessment test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check that a robot-cut layer is the right thickness at the hot-blade corner before signing the quality sheet. The trainer should let me stop the cutter when it drifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a setup posting show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted setup job must show the base rate, shift times and training required. I would keep this paid line until a real offer meets the mortgage and care costs.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes foam orders before robots cut layers around 2034.
A **recognized machine-check route** needs real paid practice and a posted role.
think: At **51**, I may still need high night wages for the mortgage.
A longer runway lets **new savings** grow only from actual paid shifts.
do: **Keep** paid cutter work and add new savings from full nights.
**Enrol** in recognized checks if fees and paid isolated practice covered.
**Apply** for posted safe local setup work if qualified, shifts cut, pay sufficient.
feel: **Anxious** about later pay cuts with time to prepare.
S3.quote: A five-year warning is useful only when the paid shifts and real course places appear.
fieldNote: She relies on **actual night wages** for new savings, not her existing reserve.
The **application** is distinct from course enrolment and requires qualification, cut hours and adequate safe local pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full night-rate cutter pay
Enrol in recognized machine-check course if funded paid isolated place offered
Apply for posted safe local setup role if qualified, shifts cut, regular hours and pay fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could plan foam orders, and capable robots around 2039 could cut and inspect mattress layers. I'd tell the crew there is time to ask who will check the first robot-made layer before we give up a good wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots reach the line. My children will be grown or nearly grown, but I will still need a wage, and the mortgage may still be there. Nine months saved now gives us room to choose, not a reason to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the high-paid cutter shift and add new savings from full wage months if bills allow. Each year I'll check actual nearby factory postings and our mortgage balance. If the company offers funded paid practical machine-check training on a stopped cutter, I'll attend; if robots later cut hours, I'll apply after qualifying only to posted safe local roles with enough base pay and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant handover, while our present pay is secure. A decade gives me time to learn slowly on a real machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record for a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a record of layer thickness at the blade's warm corner so a robot trial has something honest to compare with. A smooth screen cannot feel a thin corner through the mattress cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a future job real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local vacancy should state its pay, shift and required certificate. If it is only an advert for future possibilities, I will keep the current wage and our savings intact.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes orders before robots cut mattress layers around 2039.
The first **robot-made layer** still needs a physical thickness check.
think: At **56**, I may still need the cutter wage and mortgage payments.
Nine months of **savings** and a decade give room to choose.
do: **Keep** paid cutter shifts and add new savings from wages.
**Attend** paid isolated-cutter checks if funded place offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local work if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robots with current wages secure.
S4.quote: A smooth screen cannot feel a thin corner through the mattress cover.
fieldNote: Her **current high wage** remains valuable despite strong savings and a long runway.
Future **training and applications** stay conditional on real paid places, qualifications, cuts and suitable local pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full cutter wages when bills allow
Attend machine-check course if funded paid isolated-cutter place offered
Apply for posted safe local job if qualified, hours cut, base pay and shifts fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most. Capable foam-cutting robots around 2031 could shorten my higher-paid night shifts while warehouse machines affect my partner's work. A written crew plan, offered paid safe training and a real local job with enough base pay would help us decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the corner of a robot-cut mattress layer after the blade warms up. A mattress cover can hide a thin foam corner until a sleeper feels it.

headlineQuote: A mattress cover can hide a thin foam corner until a sleeper feels it.
portrait: **Freya**, 43, is a junior foam-cutter operator with secondary school education and a high night rate.
She and her forklift-driver partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with nine months saved.
She **never uses AI** and wants physical instruction on a stopped cutter before trusting a new machine.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about high-paid shifts despite strong savings and plentiful nearby plants.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable foam cutters around 2031 and reduce her higher-paid night shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, offered paid isolated-cutter training and posted safe local work at enough base pay would help.
